title: Oakland score pour Safe Discharge After Lower GI Bleed

how_to_use.why:
- Uses readily available demographic and clinical variables to predict both the safety of discharge and the risk of major adverse events, including major bleeding, the need for blood transfusion, or interventions to achieve hemostasis.
- Helps assess the risk of adverse outcomes and determine whether a patient is a suitable candidate for outpatient management.
how_to_use.when: In emergency department patients who present with lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB).
how_to_use.pearls:
- A score of ≤8 does not have sufficient diagnostic accuracy to independently justify discharge for outpatient work up.
- A score >8 is specific for predicting adverse events including readmission, major hemorrhage, and blood transfusion requirement; and that the patient may not be safe for discharge.

next_steps.management:
- The original score was created and validated using a cutoff of ≤8.
- Scores >8 identify high-risk patients who may need hospital admission.
- Clinical judgment should always be utilized when determining disposition planning for patients with suspected lower GI bleed.

evidence:
A network meta-analysis that included 4 trials assessed the predictive value of the Oakland score for determining safe discharge for patients with LGIB. For predicting safe discharge, an Oakland score below 8 had low sensitivity (10%, 95% CI: 5–20%) but high specificity (97%, 95% CI: 95–98%). However, the negative likelihood ratio (LR–) was 0.9, indicating poor ability to rule out unsafe discharge.

An Oakland score greater than 8 is associated with a higher risk of adverse events. For major bleeding, sensitivity was 97% (95% CI: 95–99%), specificity was 9% (95% CI: 7–12%), and a positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of 1.07. For predicting the need for blood transfusion, sensitivity reached 99% (95% CI: 99.1–99.3%), specificity 13% (95% CI: 8–18%), and LR+ was 1.14. For the need for hemostasis, the score showed a sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 81–96%), specificity 7% (95% CI: 4–12%), and an LR+ of 1.0.

The Oakland score addresses the patient-centered outcome of admission versus discharge for workup of a serious medical condition and has been validated (internally and externally). A score above 8 indicates that the patient is not suitable for discharge. Its clinical utility has been assessed in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. It has also been recommended in clinical practice guidelines to be used in clinical decision making in conjunction with patient-specific clinical characteristics.
